# The Role of Social Media in Philippine Disaster Management: A Systematic Literature Review

Maxim Alexandrite V. Inoferio <sup>1\*</sup>, Henry Joshua A. Hernandez <sup>1</sup>, Rich Angelo P. Santos <sup>1 1</sup>**De La Salle University \***[**maxim\_alexandrite\_inoferio@dlsu.edu.ph**](mailto:maxim_alexandrite_inoferio@dlsu.edu.ph)

Jeyson T. Taeza<sup>1</sup>, **Research Adviser** <sup>1</sup>**De La Salle University**

**Abstract:** Despite the Philippines being one of the world’s most disaster-prone countries, research on the role of social media in its disaster risk management remains limited. This study addresses this gap through a systematic review of existing literature on social media use in Philippine disaster risk management. The analysis is framed within the context of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC) and its four thematic areas: Prevention and Mitigation, Preparedness, Response, and Rehabilitation and Recovery, which guide disaster risk reduction efforts in the country. Results show that social media is primarily employed in response to typhoons and earthquakes, while its application to other hazards such as COVID-19, floods, and vegetation fires remains underexplored. Usage is concentrated in the response and recovery phases, with minimal attention to prevention, and no studies focused on mitigation. Notable best practices include real-time crisis monitoring through social media data, standardized emergency communication, active two-way engagement with the public, and the use of AI to detect misinformation. These practices highlight the platform’s potential to improve situational awareness and coordination. However, there is a critical need to expand research on how social media can support preparedness and mitigation, particularly in light of increasing climate risks. Incorporating sentiment analysis may also provide valuable insights into public perception, enabling more responsive and adaptive disaster strategies. Strengthening the evidence base through targeted studies can enhance the role of social media in disaster risk management frameworks and inform policy development aimed at more resilient disaster responses.

**Keywords:** disaster, risk reduction, management, social media, NDRRMC, systematic review

## 1. INTRODUCTION

The Philippines is situated where the Pacific Ring of Fire and the typhoon belt meet, making it one of the most disaster-prone countries in the world. The geographical location of the Philippines makes it highly vulnerable to strong typhoons, earthquakes, and volcanic eruptions year after year. Climate change is one of the main causes behind the increasing frequency and intensity of natural disasters in the Philippines. It has led to more extreme weather patterns, including stronger typhoons, heavier rainfall, rising sea levels, and global warming. As a result, many communities, particularly those in coastal and low-lying areas, are now at risk of flooding, sudden rise in sea level, and other types of disasters (Delfino et al., 2023; Holden & Marshall, 2018). With disasters posing constant danger to the lives of Filipinos, positioning good plans for preparedness, response, recovery, and mitigation is essential (Jha et al., 2018; Robielos et al., 2020). On average, about 20 tropical cyclones hit the country each year, with some causing severe damage (Santos, 2021). For instance, Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) 2013 affected over 16 million people, claimed more than 6,300 lives, and displaced around 4 million (Prasetyo et al., 2020). Earthquakes in the Philippines often damage homes, roads, schools, and health centers. When this happens, many families lose access to food, clean water, and medical care. For instance, the 2022 Luzon earthquake affected over 574,000 people, damaged more than 36,000 houses, and destroyed 177 health facilities (NDRRMC, 2022), leaving many families without stable shelter or reliable food sources. Disasters were linked to increased food insecurity and stunted growth in children, which are serious concerns for long-term health and development (Edwards, Gray, & Borja, 2020).

Despite the Philippines’ frequent exposure to disasters, there is a lack of studies evaluating its disaster risk reduction and management efforts, especially those utilizing social media, which inhibits a proper understanding of its strengths and weaknesses (Bollettino et al., 2020; Ner et al., 2022; Ogie et al., 2022). The gap in studies is one of multiple reasons that impact the capacity of the government, disaster response organizations, and communities to evaluate the efficacy of social media in disaster preparedness and recovery. Additionally, it is still unclear how well social media assists coordination among government agencies such as the NDRRMC and impacts people using real-time information exchange (Theda, 2024).

The NDRRMC is the Philippines’ highest policy-making organization, coordinating disaster risk reduction and management. It serves as the highest resource allocator and coordinator of all catastrophe management. The National Disaster Coordinating Council (NDCC) was the previous name of the NDRRMC. It organizes all disaster management initiatives, including those of government agencies and NGOs (National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council [NDRRMC], 2011, 2020). The NDRRMC follows four thematic areas in its disaster management plan: Prevention and Mitigation, Preparedness, Response, Rehabilitation, and Recovery. The first Thematic Area, Prevention and Mitigation, is to prevent risks and lessen the possible effects by lowering exposure and vulnerabilities and strengthening community capacities. Secondly, Preparedness aims to enhance communities' ability to prepare for, deal with, and recover from the disastrous effects of emergencies and natural disasters. The third Thematic Area, Response, focuses on preserving life and satisfying the impacted population's basic subsistence needs during or after a disaster. Finally, the fourth Thematic Area, Rehabilitation and Recovery, focuses on restoring and enhancing impacted communities' infrastructure and living while lowering the likelihood of disasters in line with the "building back better" concept (National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council [NDRRMC], 2011, 2020).

In contrast, other studies suggest a different approach to disaster management as the current form of most is still based on the four main phases: mitigation, preparedness, response, and recovery. (Sawalha, 2020) challenges the traditional disaster management phases, providing a contemporary view involving a conceptual framework, emphasizing how each disaster is dealt with, which is unique and evolving, so a new disaster management approach must also be implemented. Focusing more on a practical, proactive, and adaptive approach (Disaster Prevention and Mitigation and Disaster Preparedness), leveraging innovation or modern technology, and involving entrepreneurial and leadership mentality amongst the community during disasters will help achieve resiliency. Similarly, Oloruntoba et al. (2018) point out the need for an organized approach to disaster management. That preparedness includes proactive interventions like risk assessment, emergency planning, training, and community participation to reduce disaster risks. Successful disaster preparedness depends on early warning and partnership between government agencies, the private sector, and communities. While in the recovery phase, the emphasis is on returning to normalcy through damage assessment, infrastructure rebuilding, financial assistance, and psychological counseling. Good governance and policies are essential in facilitating a seamless and sustainable recovery. Through the incorporation of best practices from diverse disaster management models, the outlined framework encourages collaboration, adaptability, and continuous improvement. Ultimately, it will serve as a proposed guide for policymakers, emergency workers, and communities to advance disaster resilience and response activities.

In recent years, social media has become a vital tool for disaster preparedness, response, and recovery. Platforms like Twitter and Facebook allow communities, humanitarian organizations, and government agencies to share real-time updates, like evacuation plans, early warnings, and relief efforts (Del Icalla, 2025). Compared to traditional media, social media provides immediate two-way communication, allowing people to report local events, locate missing persons, and request assistance during disasters (Congjuico, 2014). Studies conducted by Demiroz & Akbas (2020) highlight social media as essential in organizing volunteers, coordinating emergency responses, and collecting donations. Social media helps people and provides insight into the long-term needs of disaster victims. Social media, for instance, was found to help monitor shifts in people's needs during Typhoon Haiyan, including requests for housing aid and relief supplies (Takahashi & Tandoc, 2014).

In addition to supporting response efforts, social media is useful for understanding public emotions during disasters. In a study by Shapouri, S., Soleymani, S., & Rezayi, S. (2024), Twitter data could track how people’s emotions changed over time, helping responders understand how communities react to disasters.

A growing body of research explores the significant potential of social media in disaster management and response. However, most existing studies have primarily examined its use during the emergency management and initial disaster response phases, particularly in enhancing situational awareness. Notably, these studies have mainly focused on other countries, with limited research conducted in the Philippine context. Existing systematic reviews have several gaps that limit a complete understanding of how social media is utilized in disaster management. Wiegmann et al. (2021) and Amiresmaili et al. (2021) discuss the role of social media in improving disaster response by filling information gaps and enhancing situational awareness. However, the study only addressed the potential of social media and did not provide evidence of its effectiveness in practice. Additionally, while the review mentions the potential of social media, information is not provided on how social media can be integrated with official disaster response strategies. The study of Ulvi et al. (2019) and

Amiresmaili et al. (2021) notes that social media is essential in spreading critical information and assisting relief efforts. However, the paper did not examine which social media platforms, such as Twitter or Facebook, are most effective. Furthermore, both studies mainly focus on crisis communication and response but do not analyze long-term recovery.

Social media has emerged as an essential disaster recovery tool, enabling individuals to share information, organize volunteers, and evaluate damage. Facebook and Twitter facilitate aid mobilization, enhance situational awareness, and unite responders with affected communities. Most research centers on short-term disaster response, with little attention to long-term recovery, economic rebuilding, and mental health support.

Ogie et al. (2022) and Wiegmann et al. (2021) note that disaster recovery receives much less research attention than preparedness and response. Despite the ability of social media to trace financial assistance, economic restoration, and mental health services, there are still issues such as misinformation, poor data quality, and geographic bias. Most studies concentrate on North America without considering disaster-affected regions such as the Philippines. Furthermore, more recent platforms such as TikTok, WhatsApp, and Messenger, which are used extensively for people-led disaster response, tend to be overlooked in studies. The absence of data verification also leads to concerns over misinformation and credibility. Tan et al. (2017) explain how mobile applications aid disaster management but emphasize that app effectiveness and user engagement require more research. It was also pointed out that there is a need for usability and verification systems to provide accurate information. Crisis informatics studies indicate that disaster communication is transitioning from top-down to more participatory, citizen-led approaches. To fully maximize the potential of social media in disaster recovery, future studies need to advance data validation, broaden studies to underrepresented areas, and investigate its application in ecological recovery and animal welfare. Filling these gaps will improve long-term disaster resilience, particularly in vulnerable populations.

In this context, this study aims to examine the current research on the roles of social media in disaster management in the Philippines, identify its specific functions and strategies, explore how social media platforms improve disaster response efforts, and highlight emerging gaps in the existing research landscape.

## 2. METHODOLOGY

This study conducted a systematic review to critically examine the role of social media in disaster-related contexts in the Philippines. A systematic review is a rigorous, transparent, and replicable method of synthesizing existing research by adhering to a predefined protocol that ensures the comprehensive identification, evaluation, and integration of relevant literature. This approach employs a structured search strategy, explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria, and a critical appraisal of the quality and relevance of selected studies. A systematic review facilitates the identification of gaps, deficiencies, and emerging trends in the existing literature, thereby contributing to the development of future research directions and evidence-based advancements in the field (Munn et al., 2018).

The review process was guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) framework (Moher et al., 2009), which consists of four key phases: Identification, Screening, Eligibility, and Inclusion. This standardized approach ensured a transparent, methodical, and replicable selection of relevant literature.

To achieve a comprehensive review, relevant studies were sourced from three major academic databases: Google Scholar, Scopus, and ScienceDirect. These databases were selected due to their extensive coverage of peer-reviewed publications across diverse disciplines, ensuring a broad and representative collection of scholarly research. Only articles published between January 1, 2015, and December 31, 2024, were considered to ensure the review reflects the most recent and relevant research.

## Figure 1

**Annual Inventory of Published Articles** entries. During the Screening phase, exclusion criteria were systematically applied to refine the dataset. First, non-journal articles such as conference papers, book chapters, book reviews, and commentaries (n = 64) were excluded to ensure academic rigor by focusing solely on peer-reviewed studies. Second, research not based in the Philippines (n = 610) was removed to maintain the study’s geographic relevance. Third, articles that did not explicitly examine the intersection of social media and disasters (n = 295) were excluded to align with the research objectives.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

In the identification phase, an initial search retrieved 1,006 unique records after removing duplicate

The eligibility phase involved further refinement, ensuring that only empirical studies utilizing social media content as a primary data source were retained. Studies failing to meet this criterion were excluded. Finally, 18 articles were selected for in-depth analysis in the Inclusion phase. These studies were systematically reviewed to extract key themes, methodologies, and findings concerning the role of social media in disaster preparedness, response, and recovery within the Philippine context. By adopting this rigorous and methodical approach, the study provides a comprehensive synthesis of existing research, offering valuable insights into how social media is leveraged in disaster-related situations in the Philippines.

## 3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

## 3.1. Summary of Data

Among the 19 uses of social media, based on Figure 3, the most used social media platform is Twitter, with 15 uses. The articles of Graham et al. (2015), Cheng et al. (2019), and Takahashi et al. (2015) looked at tweets during Typhoon Haiyan to understand how people shared information and worked together to coordinate relief efforts. Additionally, some researchers combined Twitter data with other tools. Jongman et al. (2015) used tweets and satellite images to track floods, while Bakillah et al. (2014) used Twitter to map out online communities that helped report disaster-related issues. Furthermore, Zhang and Cheng (2021) focused on whether tweets were positive or negative, which helped understand public sentiment during disasters. Similarly, Kupsch (2017) and Maceda et al. (2017) separated tweets into informative and conversational to separate helpful disaster updates from personal thoughts. This helps focus on important information while still understanding public sentiment. At the same time, David et al. (2016) found that retweets usually shared facts like news or official updates, while regular tweets showed more personal sentiments. Furthermore, Twitter was also used to track other issues like public reactions to COVID-19 (Owuor & Hochmair, 2023) and the effects of smoke pollution (Du et al., 2024). Moreover, the second most used platform within the studies was Facebook, with 2 uses. Lai et al. (2017) studied how relief groups connected after Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda), and Velasco (2021) looked at how people reacted to animals being left behind during Typhoon Vamco (Ulysses). The least used social media platforms are TikTok and Flickr, which were used 2 times. Berdida et al. (2022) analyzed comments of Filipinos on TikTok videos regarding vaccine-related videos to understand why some Filipinos hesitated to get COVID-19 vaccines. In another study, Yan et al. (2017) used geotagged photos on Flickr to assess and monitor the post-disaster tourism recovery in areas recovered after the Bohol earthquake and Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda).

Out of the 19 identified frequency of disaster types in the reviewed articles, 12 focused on typhoons (63.2%), making it the most studied type of disaster: (Graham et al., 2015; Cheng et al., 2019; Takahashi et al., 2015; Lai et al., 2017; Bakillah et al., 2015; Yan et al., 2017; Soriano et al., 2016; Malawani et al., 2020; Velasco, 2021; Shen et al., 2021; Zhang & Cheng, 2021; David et al., 2016). Studies focused on emergency management, real-time damage assessment, population movement, and public sentiment during and after the typhoon. Earthquakes with 3 (15.8%): (Kupsch, 2017; Maceda et al., 2017; Yan et al., 2017) were studied for the immediate impact, including building collapses and economic losses, with social media data used to track damage and recovery, particularly in tourism. COVID-19 with 2 (10.5%): (Berdida et al., 2022; Owuor & Hochmair, 2023) focused on the pandemic's effects on public health, vaccine hesitancy, and the relationship between social media mentions and COVID-19 news reports. Floods with 1 (5.3%): (Jongman et al., 2015) examined how social media and satellite data were used for early flood detection and real-time reporting. Vegetation fires with 1 (5.3%): (Du et al., 2024) studied public sentiment regarding fire smoke and its environmental impacts, focusing on social media responses to air quality concerns.

## 3.2. Uses of Social Media in Disaster Management Phases in the Philippines

## 3.2.1. Response

Social media has become an essential resource for disaster response in the Philippines, allowing real-time exchange of information, emotional connection, and relief efforts. Nevertheless, its usefulness is limited by misinformation, noise in data, and infrastructure constraints. These platforms allowed affected parties to post needs and assisted responders in tracking damage and coordinating relief during crises like Typhoon Haiyan and COVID-19 (Takahashi et al., 2015; David et al., 2016; Berdida et al., 2022). However, Graham et al. (2015) indicated that 13.5% of tweets gathered were pertinent, only 1.5% geolocated, reflecting the paucity of local information resulting from impaired communications. Similarly, Kupsch (2017) emphasized filtering irrelevant posts by distinguishing between “informative” and “conversational” tweets. Malawani et al. (2020) and Berdida et al. (2023) warned of the dangers of misinformation and disinformation, which can quickly spread fear and confusion during crises. Research indicates that hybrid frameworks that integrate social media analysis with satellite imagery enhance disaster monitoring and early warning (Jongman et al., 2015; Du et al., 2024), whereas innovations such as the Normalized Affected Population Index (NAPI) provide near-real-time location-based observations that closely match government impact data (Cheng et al., 2019). Lai et al. (2017) and Maceda et al. (2017) discovered that although social media improved situational awareness and facilitated the location of missing individuals, NGOs and journalists were leading relief coordination, while government agencies tended to concentrate on reporting rather than real-time planning. Similarly, Soriano et al. (2016) noted that 60% of Typhoon Haiyan tweets were civic, encompassing solidarity, charity drives, and political commentary, but a mere fraction coordinated rescue or relief. Despite these constraints, research such as that of Bakillah et al. (2015) illustrated that clustering geo-tagged tweets can discern communities discussing specific disaster-related topics. Shen et al. (2021) and Zhang and Cheng (2021) pointed out Twitter's function to heighten global attention and monitor public opinion, albeit with a warning against privacy threats and language prejudices. Velasco (2021) demonstrated how viral Facebook posts during Typhoon Vamco activated public outrage regarding animal welfare, demonstrating the website's potential to advocate for policy reforms. Owuor and Hochmair (2023) observed that in a few instances, surges in social media traffic occurred before official COVID-19 case reports, highlighting its potential as an early warning system, although with regional variations and quality of data. These observations highlight social media's revolutionary but multifaceted role in disaster relief as it speeds up communication and participation.

## 3.2.2 Recovery

Social media, particularly Twitter and Facebook, were essential platforms for spreading disaster-related information like warnings, safety protocols, and ongoing recovery efforts. Through real-time posts from both government agencies and civilians, these platforms became vital tools for keeping communities informed (Graham et al., 2015; Takahashi et al., 2015; Soriano et al., 2016; David et al., 2016; Shen et al., 2021). Additionally, Graham et al. (2015), Takahashi et al. (2015), Lai et al. (2017), Malawani et al. (2020), Shen et al. (2021), and David et al. (2016) discussed how social media was used for better coordination among relief organizations by providing a platform for tracking the needed resources and volunteer efforts. In particular, Takahashi et al. (2015) discussed how organizations used Twitter to communicate the urgent resources required. For example, tweets from relief groups provided real-time updates on the supply shortages, which promoted faster responses from donors and volunteers. Furthermore, geotagging was also utilized from social media posts such as tweets and Flickr images to assess the damage done by disasters. By mapping location-based posts, it was identified which area had the most damage and monitored how the communities gradually recovered. (Bakillah et al., 2014; Yan et al., 2017; Shen et al., 2021; Zhang & Cheng, 2021) In addition, the article by Lai et al. (2017) found that government agencies often served as key coordination points that allowed the spread of information, while organizations helped spread this information through retweets. Furthermore, Yan et al. (2017) analyzed photos shared on Flickr about the changes in tourism activity following a disaster. Tourism-related posts, in terms of their volume and location, provided insights into the pace of recovery in disaster-hit areas by indicating levels of tourist interest and signs of economic revival. Unlike other studies that focused on community recovery, Valesco (2021) examined how social media raised awareness about animals abandoned during disasters. The study showed that Facebook helped coordinate rescue efforts and encouraged more people to donate to animal shelters. However, only a few studies directly focused on restoring livelihoods, infrastructure, shelter, or the physical and psychological rehabilitation of individuals affected by disasters. Malawani et al. (2020) best addressed objectives on rehabilitation and recovery by tracking the changing priorities of Typhoon Washi (Sendong) victims, which include calls for housing, medical supplies, and sustained relief, while also addressing the gaps in government rehousing efforts. Yan et al. (2017) examined tourism recovery in disaster-affected areas by using geo-tagged photos to track economic activity and the speed of infrastructure repairs in popular tourist locations. Meanwhile, Soriano et al. (2016) indirectly addressed livelihood restoration by highlighting civic engagement and fundraising efforts that supported both immediate and long-term recovery. In contrast, the remaining studies by Graham et al. (2015), Shen et al. (2021), Takahashi et al. (2015), David et al. (2016), Zhang & Cheng (2021), Lai et al. (2017), Bakillah et al. (2014), and Velasco (2021) mainly focused on social media usage, content types, information distribution, public sentiment, community engagement, and communication networks during disasters. This shows that more studies should look at how social media can help not just during disasters, but also in long-term recovery, such as rebuilding lives and communities.

## 3.2.3 Preparedness

Similar to how social media plays a significant role in disaster response and recovery, it also helps people be prepared before it happens. It does this by helping professionals evaluate past events to improve safety drills and warning systems. For instance, Maceda et al. (2017) discovered that many people were unprepared in the study of tweets related to earthquakes, highlighting the need for improved earthquake drills and early warning systems. The study examined Twitter data following a major earthquake in the Philippines and found that people's responses were frequently unclear or uninformed, with few mentions of safety precautions. This showed a lack of public awareness, indicating that communities could benefit from targeted safety education on social media to improve preparedness for future disasters. A related study by Berdida et al. (2022), monitoring TikTok comments about vaccine hesitancy, helped health officials create better campaigns to educate people before an emergency. The study observed how easily false health information spread on the platform, influencing public perceptions and behavior regarding vaccination. By identifying trends and common concerns within user comments, public health workers could adjust the messages to correct false information and build trust in medical advice before the outbreak became more serious. While both studies contribute to increasing community awareness of hazards and risks, the studies leave important points of preparedness that are rarely addressed. In the study of Maceda et al. (2017), the focus on public confusion after an earthquake highlights that there is a clear need for more education, but the study gives limited information on how this awareness leads to useful skills, stronger institutions, or collaborative efforts. Similarly, Berdida et al. (2022) show that monitoring TikTok comments can help shape health education campaigns, but it is not clear if these efforts helped improve how people respond to health emergencies or encouraged teamwork between government, health services, and media groups. In both examples, social media is used to inform the public, but its part in building long-term preparedness or supporting strong partnerships is not clearly shown. In another example, Soriano et al. (2016) mentioned that during Typhoon Yolanda, Twitter played a significant role in raising awareness, especially with the help of celebrities and influencers, who encouraged people to take disaster preparation seriously. The analysis showed how tweets from high-profile figures gained more engagement, helping spread official warnings and encouraging people to take action, such as stocking supplies, creating evacuation plans, or attending preparedness seminars. The study helps support the goal of increasing public awareness and shows how social media can motivate people to take real steps to prepare for disasters. Still, similar to the earlier studies by Berdida et al. (2022) and Maceda et al. (2017), it does not clearly show how these actions were supported by government institutions, guided by formal preparedness plans, or linked to long-term policy development. Although these studies emphasize the use of digital platforms for information sharing and clearing up false information, they provide limited detail about how these practices might fit into larger systems for disaster preparedness. How emergency responders, local governments, and health services support or sustain these efforts, or how to transform public engagement into long-term projects, is not widely recognized. Social media use increases awareness and encourages early action, but it is also important to decide whether it builds up connections among important stakeholders and enhances organizations' capacity to handle risks in the future. There has been little discussion of how this early information was integrated into official disaster planning or how it resulted in coordinated responses, even in the case of Owuor and Hochmair (2023), where it was demonstrated that social media could predict an increase in COVID-19 cases. In the study of Owuor and Hochmair (2023) found that an increase in tweets about COVID-19 often came before a rise in actual cases, showing that social media could act as an early warning tool for pandemics and other emergencies. By analyzing geotagged Twitter data, it was shown that changes in what people were saying online often happened before actual case numbers increased, giving officials time to share health warnings or get ready. This ability to predict problems could also be useful for other types of emergencies, making it a helpful part of disaster preparedness. Although the study highlights the value of early awareness, it gives little detail on how this awareness leads to community training or how organizations use it in disaster planning. Additionally, the study provides little insight into whether organizations like emergency response organizations, health agencies, and social media platforms work together to turn this data into coordinated actions. These gaps suggest that while social media is useful for raising awareness and sharing warnings, more research is needed to see how it can be better connected to formal systems of disaster preparedness. Beyond awareness and education, social media also has predictive value.

## 3.3 Research Gaps and Recommendations for Future Studies

This section outlines several essential research gaps revealed through the review and points out potential directions for future studies in this area. The most significant is an absence of attention to mitigation since none of the studies investigate long-term measures to prevent disasters and reduce risks. Although response and recovery thematic areas are somehow addressed, topics such as misinformation management, social media's impact on public confidence in disaster agencies, and economic and infrastructure recovery are vaguely discussed during these two phases. Moreover, most existing research focuses on Twitter, with gaps in how other social media platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and WhatsApp play roles in disaster communication before, during, and even after. Relevant to types of disasters, most studies discussed the 2013 Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda), hence this paper suggests looking more into recent notable typhoons (e.g. Typhoon Odette in 2021, Typhoon Pepito in 2024), as well as other disaster types ranging from earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and drought since social media continues to develop, as do the platforms and the usage in disaster management. There is also scant research on socioeconomic inequalities in disaster response, especially how various groups access and use emergency information available on social media. It is suggested that social media be integrated into conventional disaster alert systems, policy guidelines for government utilization of social media for crisis communication be framed, and strategies against misinformation should be strengthened by collaboration among the government and LGUs, especially the NDRRMC, as the primary government body responsible for disaster management efforts. Another fundamental suggestion is to look into the public's trust in disaster organizations and how digital interaction affects the perception of response capability. As discussed above, there is a lack of focus on using social media during the mitigation phase of disaster management. Future studies are encouraged to explore how social media can support proactive measures such as risk reduction, hazard awareness campaigns, and strengthening community resilience to minimize long-term risks from incoming disasters. It is also recommended that researchers undertake meta-analyses to systematically examine trends, best practices, and gaps in the application of social media across all phases of disaster management. Such analyses provide valuable statistical insights and help ensure a more balanced research focus beyond response and recovery. Existing literature highlights the best practices, such as leveraging social media data for real-time crisis monitoring, establishing standardized emergency communication protocols, fostering active public engagement through two-way communication, and implementing AI-powered misinformation detection systems. Policymakers are also encouraged to utilize social media-based sentiment analysis to understand public concerns better and refine disaster preparedness and response strategies. Furthermore, future studies in the Philippine context should incorporate the Filipino language when analyzing social media data, as this can provide a more accurate representation of public sentiment and community needs. Addressing these gaps through localized and technologically innovative research approaches can strengthen the role of social media in disaster management and enhance its effectiveness in mitigating risks.

## 4. CONCLUSIONS

This study has presented findings from a systematic literature review on the use of social media in disaster management in the Philippines. The review aimed to provide a clear overview of how online platforms have been used to support different phases of disaster response, recovery, and preparedness. A total of 18 peer-reviewed articles published between 2015 and 2024 were analyzed, focusing specifically on disasters that occurred in the Philippines and used social media as the primary data source. The findings show that social media plays a significant role in the response phase of disaster management, with Twitter being one of the most commonly studied platforms, followed by Facebook. In contrast, other platforms like TikTok and Flickr had limited attention. Most studies focused on typhoons, and fewer on other disasters like floods, earthquakes, public health emergencies like COVID-19, and fires. Throughout these disasters, social media was used for real-time communication, coordination, and public insight. Despite these findings, important gaps remain. Most studies focus on the response and recovery phases, with little research on preparedness and none on mitigation. This review concludes with a few recommendations for future research. There is a need to examine lesser-studied social media platforms and disaster types, develop more effective approaches to managing misinformation, and explore how social media can be more effectively connected to disaster-related policies and practices. Addressing these areas can help improve how social media is used in disaster management in the Philippines.
